chunks.heading: What does a < b really mean?
chunks.body: Saying a is less than b means a sits to the left of b on the number line. It also means that b minus a is a positive number.

chunks.heading: Solving simple inequations
chunks.body: Solve an inequation the same way as an equation: add, subtract, multiply, divide both sides. But flip the inequality sign whenever you multiply or divide by a negative number.
chunks.checkText: When do you flip an inequality sign?

checkOptions.text: When multiplying or dividing by a negative number
Never — the sign always stays the same

chunks.heading: Solving inequations with a parabola
chunks.body: To solve a quadratic inequation, move everything to one side, then sketch the parabola. Read the solution straight from where the graph is above or below the x-axis.
chunks.checkText: To solve a quadratic inequation by graphing, you first...

checkOptions.text: Move all terms to one side

chunks.heading: Absolute value as distance
chunks.body: |x − b| = a means the distance from x to b is a. You can solve absolute value equations and inequations by picturing this distance on a number line.

checkOptions.text: Value of b divided by x

chunks.heading: Inequations with x in the denominator
chunks.body: Multiplying both sides by an unknown denominator is risky, because you don't know if it's positive or negative. Instead, multiply both sides by the square of the denominator, which is never negative.
chunks.checkText: Why multiply by the square of the denominator, not the denominator itself?

checkOptions.text: Because the square is never negative, so the inequality sign never flips
Because it makes the equation shorter
Because squaring removes all fractions instantly

chunks.heading: Where can a function change sign?
chunks.body: A function can only switch from positive to negative, or back, at a zero or at a discontinuity — a point where its graph breaks. Nowhere else.

chunks.heading: Building a table of signs
chunks.body: List the zeroes and discontinuities of a function in order, then test a value between and around each one. Record whether the function is positive or negative at each test point.
chunks.checkText: A table of signs uses test values that...

checkOptions.text: Dodge around the zeroes and discontinuities
Are chosen at random with no pattern

chunks.heading: Solving inequations using a table of signs
chunks.body: Once a [[mathext1-table-of-signs|table of signs]] is built, reading off where the function is positive or negative directly solves the inequation — no graph needed.
chunks.checkText: A table of signs lets you solve an inequation by...

checkOptions.text: Reading off where the function is positive or negative
Always setting the function equal to zero

chunks.heading: Two rules about reciprocals
chunks.body: The reciprocal of a very small number is very large, and the reciprocal of a very large number is very small. Also, the reciprocal of a positive number stays positive.

chunks.heading: Spotting a vertical asymptote
chunks.body: If a function's denominator is zero at x = a, but its numerator isn't zero there, then x = a is a vertical asymptote.

checkOptions.text: Denominator is zero but the numerator isn't

chunks.heading: Reciprocal graphs keep the same sign
chunks.body: The graph of 1/f(x) is positive wherever f(x) is positive, and negative wherever f(x) is negative. Taking a reciprocal never flips the sign.

chunks.body: Every zero of f(x) becomes a vertical asymptote of 1/f(x). Every vertical asymptote of f(x) becomes a zero of 1/f(x), with that point removed.

chunks.heading: What happens far from the origin
chunks.body: If f(x) grows towards infinity as x gets large, then 1/f(x) shrinks towards zero. This gives the reciprocal graph a horizontal asymptote.

chunks.body: The ordinate of a point is just another name for its y-coordinate. It's a handy shorthand when combining graphs.

chunks.body: If f(x) has a zero at x = a, then at that point the sum s(x) = f(x) + g(x) equals g(a). So the sum's graph meets g(x) exactly there.

chunks.heading: What absolute value means
chunks.body: The absolute value |x| equals x when x is zero or positive, and equals −x when x is negative. It's always zero or positive, never negative.

checkOptions.text: Always equal to the number itself

chunks.body: Keep every part of the graph that's already above the x-axis. Reflect any part below the x-axis upward, so nothing ends up negative.

Reflect the whole graph in the y-axis

chunks.body: Keep the part of the graph to the right of the y-axis unchanged. Replace everything to the left with a mirror copy of the right-hand side.

chunks.heading: What the inverse relation is
chunks.body: The inverse relation of any relation is found by swapping the x and y in every ordered pair. Reversing the reversed pairs gets you back to the original.
chunks.checkText: The inverse relation is formed by...

checkOptions.text: Swapping x and y in every ordered pair

chunks.heading: Graphing the inverse
chunks.body: The graph of the [[mathext1-inverse-relation-definition|inverse relation]] is just the original graph reflected in the diagonal line y = x.

chunks.heading: Domain and range swap places
chunks.body: Because the coordinates are swapped, the domain of the inverse relation is the range of the original. Likewise, the range of the inverse is the original's domain.
chunks.checkText: The domain of the inverse relation equals the...

checkOptions.text: Set of all real numbers, always

chunks.heading: Finding the inverse's equation
chunks.body: To find the equation of an inverse relation, write x for y and y for x everywhere they appear, then solve for y if you can.

checkOptions.text: Swap x and y everywhere, then solve for y

chunks.heading: Is the inverse a function?
chunks.body: The inverse relation is a function only if every horizontal line crosses the original graph at most once. This is called the horizontal line test.

The original relation is a function

chunks.heading: Writing the inverse function
chunks.body: When a function's inverse is also a function, it's written f⁻¹(x). Be careful: this is not the same as 1/f(x), even though the notation looks similar.

chunks.heading: Undoing a function with its inverse
chunks.body: Applying a function and then its inverse always gets you back to where you started: f⁻¹(f(x)) = x and f(f⁻¹(x)) = x.

chunks.heading: Restricting a domain to get an inverse
chunks.body: A many-to-one function fails the [[mathext1-horizontal-line-test|horizontal line test]], so its inverse relation isn't a function. Restricting the domain can make the function one-to-one, giving it a genuine inverse function.

checkOptions.text: Make it one-to-one, so it has an inverse function
Make its graph a straight line

chunks.heading: What a parameter is
chunks.body: A parameter is an extra variable, often called t, used to write both x and y as separate functions. Each value of t gives one point on the curve.

chunks.body: Eliminating the [[mathext1-parameter-definition|parameter]] means combining the two parametric equations to produce a single Cartesian equation relating x and y directly.

chunks.body: The circle x² + y² = r² can be written as x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ. This works because cos²θ + sin²θ = 1.

chunks.heading: What is a polynomial?
chunks.body: A polynomial is an expression made by adding whole-number powers of x, each multiplied by a constant. There are no square roots or fractional powers of x allowed.

checkOptions.text: Fractional powers of x, like x^(1/2)

chunks.heading: Degree and leading term
chunks.body: The term with the highest power of x is called the leading term, and its coefficient is the leading coefficient. The value of that highest power is the polynomial's degree.
chunks.checkText: The degree of a polynomial is the...

checkOptions.text: Highest power of x with a nonzero coefficient

chunks.heading: Monic polynomials
chunks.body: A polynomial is called monic if its [[mathext1-degree-leading-term|leading coefficient]] is exactly 1. For example, x³ − 2x² + 4 is monic, but 3x² + 1 is not.

chunks.heading: Names for low-degree polynomials
chunks.body: A degree-1 polynomial is linear, degree-2 is quadratic, degree-3 is cubic, and degree-4 is quartic. These names describe the polynomial's degree.
chunks.checkText: A polynomial of degree 3 is called a...

chunks.heading: When two polynomials are truly equal
chunks.body: Two polynomials are identically equal if they give the same value for every possible x, not just some values. When this happens, their matching coefficients must also be equal.
chunks.checkText: If two polynomials are identically equal, then their...

chunks.heading: How a polynomial behaves far out
chunks.body: For very large or very negative x, a polynomial's graph is controlled entirely by its [[mathext1-degree-leading-term|leading term]]. Every other term becomes too small to matter.
chunks.checkText: Far from the origin, a polynomial's graph is controlled by its...

chunks.heading: Odd-degree polynomials always cross zero
chunks.body: A polynomial of odd degree heads towards +∞ on one side and −∞ on the other. Because its graph is unbroken, it must cross the x-axis somewhere.
chunks.checkText: Every polynomial of odd degree has at least one...

chunks.heading: What multiplicity means
chunks.body: If the factor (x − α) appears m times in a polynomial, then α is called a zero of multiplicity m. A repeated factor means a repeated zero.

chunks.heading: Even multiplicity: a turning point
chunks.body: At a zero with even [[mathext1-multiplicity-of-zero|multiplicity]], the curve touches the x-axis and turns back without crossing it. This point is called a turning point.

checkOptions.text: Touches the x-axis and turns back

chunks.heading: Odd multiplicity of 3 or more: horizontal inflection
chunks.body: At a zero with odd multiplicity of 3 or higher, the curve flattens against the x-axis but still crosses it. This flat crossing is called a horizontal inflection.

chunks.heading: Simple zeroes: a clean crossing
chunks.body: A zero of multiplicity 1 is called a simple zero. At a simple zero, the curve crosses the x-axis cleanly, with no flattening or turning.

chunks.heading: The result of dividing polynomials
chunks.body: Dividing one polynomial by another gives a quotient and a remainder, just like dividing whole numbers. This is written as dividend = divisor × quotient + remainder.

chunks.heading: How big can the remainder be?
chunks.body: After dividing polynomials, the remainder is either the zero polynomial, or it has a smaller degree than the divisor. The division can't continue any further than that.
chunks.checkText: After polynomial division, the remainder's degree must be...

checkOptions.text: Smaller than the divisor's degree, or the remainder is zero

chunks.heading: Long dividing polynomials
chunks.body: Divide the leading term of what's left by the leading term of the divisor, multiply back, and subtract. Repeat this until nothing more can be divided.

chunks.heading: The remainder theorem
chunks.body: The remainder theorem says that dividing a polynomial P(x) by (x − α) leaves a remainder equal to P(α). No long division is needed to find it.

chunks.heading: The factor theorem
chunks.body: The [[mathext1-remainder-theorem|remainder theorem]] tells us that (x − α) is a factor of P(x) exactly when P(α) = 0. This gives a quick test for factors.

chunks.heading: Testing for integer zeroes
chunks.body: If every coefficient of a polynomial is a whole number, then any whole-number zero must be a divisor of the constant term. This narrows down what to test.

chunks.heading: Factoring using the factor theorem
chunks.body: Test possible integer zeroes using the [[mathext1-integer-zero-test|constant term's divisors]]. Once a zero is found, use the [[mathext1-factor-theorem|factor theorem]] and long division to pull out that factor.

chunks.heading: The most zeroes a polynomial can have
chunks.body: A polynomial of degree n can have at most n zeroes. Having more than n would force it to be divisible by a polynomial of higher degree, which is impossible.

chunks.heading: Finding several zeroes at once
chunks.body: If several zeroes of a polynomial are found by trial and error, you can divide by the product of their factors in one step, instead of dividing repeatedly.

chunks.heading: Tangents are double roots
chunks.body: When a line meets a curve, solving them together gives an equation whose roots are the meeting points. If the line is a tangent, one of those roots is repeated.

chunks.body: If two curves meet at points with x-coordinates α and β, the midpoint's x-coordinate is just (α + β)/2 — found instantly using the [[mathext1-sum-product-quadratic-zeroes|sum of roots]].
